entries.subject: Creole English

spans.text: San Andres-Providence Creole English is spoken in the archipelago of San Andres, Providencia and Santa Catalina, Colombia.

entries.description: which are located off the coast of Nicaragua
entries.subject: which
entries.object: located off the coast of Nicaragua

spans.text: The archipelago consists of the island of San Andres and the two islands of Providencia (also called Old Providence) and Santa Catalina, which are located off the coast of Nicaragua, far from the Colombian mainland.

spans.text: The language is also spoken by diaspora communities, of which the one in mainland Colombia is the most important, followed by communities on the Central American Caribbean Coast, especially in Panama, and in the United States.

entries.object: San Andres Creole English (or Saintandrewan) and Providence Creole English

spans.text: The two main varieties of the language are San Andres Creole English (or Saintandrewan) and Providence Creole English.

entries.description: they are structurally distinct varieties
entries.subject: they

spans.text: However, they are structurally distinct varieties, and I believe that sociolectal variation in terms of a hypothetical creole continuum constitutes an even more important criterion: Providence Creole English is clearly a more acrolectal variety of Western Caribbean Creole English than San Andres Creole English (Bartens 2009a).

spans.text: However, these colonies were fairly short-lived: Henrietta, at present called San Andres, was abandoned in 1632 because of the lack of sweet water reservoirs on the island.

entries.subject: San Andres

spans.text: In 1793, the population of San Andres consisted of several families and 285 slaves (Parsons 1985: 48, 50).

entries.description: Slaves continued to be shipped in directly from Africa
entries.subject: Slaves
entries.object: to be shipped in directly from Africa

spans.text: Slaves continued to be shipped in directly from Africa, other British Caribbean islands and, most importantly, from Jamaica, in order to cultivate cotton, thus establishing an important historical link with Jamaica and Jamaican Creole (cf. Edwards 1970: 29).

spans.text: After the abolition of slavery in the archipelago in 1853, many Sanandresans and Providence Islanders were recruited to work on the Miskito Coast.

spans.text: According the 2005 census report, the population of San Andres is 55,426 and the one of Providencia 4,147, totalling 59,573 inhabitants (DANE 2005).

spans.text: Native Islander activists consider the figures far too low, at least as far as San Andres is concerned, where the Native Islander community clearly constitutes a minority, numbering approximately 20,000.
